claim: The survey was sent to the leaders of 1000 core facilities in different fields of the life sciences in Europe.
source: Our survey was sent to the leaders of 1000 core facilities in different fields of the life sciences in Europe.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the survey distribution method and target population.

claim: 253 complete forms were received from over 30 types of facility.
source: In total, we received 253 complete forms from over 30 types of facility, which differ in the techniques and expertise they offer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states the number of responses and references a figure showing facility types.

claim: Microscopy and FACS facilities were the most common types among respondents.
source: When ranked by types of facility, microscopy and FACS facilities were top, followed by genomics and proteomics.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the ranking of facility types.

claim: Most responses came from hybrid-service facilities, followed by full-service facilities and then self-service facilities.
source: Most of the responses to our survey came from hybrid-service facilities, followed by full-service facilities and then self-service facilities (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript states the distribution of responses by operating mode and references Figure 1A.

claim: Only about a quarter of self-service facilities keep documentation of experiments compared to >95% of full-service facilities.
source: Only about a quarter of self-service facilities keeps documentation of the experiments compared to >95% of full-service facilities.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages for documentation practices by facility type.

claim: Storage of raw data is offered by only 40% of self-service facilities compared to 82% of full-service facilities.
source: Similarly, storage of raw data is offered by only half as many self-service facilities (40%) compared to full-service facilities (82%).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages for data storage practices.

claim: Only about half of the facilities were fully aware of the NIH guidelines existence according to the ABRF survey.
source: The survey revealed that only about half of the facilities were fully aware of the NIH guidelines existence.
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from the ABRF survey.

claim: The lack of funding was cited as the most frequently encountered challenge by core facilities.
source: When asked about the biggest challenges encountered by core facilities, the most frequently cited was the lack of funding, closely followed by the lack of staff (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript states the ranking of challenges and references Figure 2B.

claim: Experiments are often performed without replication at core facilities.
source: We observe that experiments are often performed without replication, which is essential for good quality research (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and references Figure 2C.

claim: Core facilities often do not know what controls were included in experiments.
source: When it comes to experimental controls, core facilities often do not know what controls were included (Figure 2D), even though experiments lacking appropriate controls cannot be meaningfully evaluated.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 2D.

claim: 50% of self-service facilities and 13% of full-service facilities often or always allow users to analyze samples of inadequate quality.
source: When asked if users could proceed with samples of poor quality, we found that 50% of self-service and 13% of full-service facilities often or always allow users to analyze samples of inadequate quality (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages for this practice.

claim: 40% of full-service facilities and only 10% of self-service facilities have mechanisms to ensure correct analysis and interpretation of raw data.
source: Regarding the data analysis, 40% of full-service facilities and only 10% of self-service facilities have mechanisms to ensure correct analysis and interpretation of raw data (Figure 2F).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages for quality control mechanisms.

claim: 91% of all core facilities believe that if they were involved in the publication process it would improve the quality of published data.
source: The vast majority (91%) of all core facilities believe that if they were involved in the publication process it would improve the quality of published data (Figure 2G).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific percentage for this belief.

claim: Close to 30% of facilities use a management software and further 34% believe it would make sense to use one.
source: Overall, close to 30% of facilities use a management software and further 34% believe it would make sense to use one (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages for management software usage.

claim: Data management plans are used in 30% of full-service facilities but only 10% of self-service facilities.
source: Data management plans ensure that all data remain traceable, and are used in 30% of full-service facilities but only 10% of self-service facilities (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages for data management plan usage.

claim: 72% of all core facilities do not have a system to identify raw data used for published figures.
source: Strikingly, 72% of all core facilities do not have a system to identify raw data used for published figures (85% and 63% for self-service and full-service respectively; Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages for data traceability systems.

claim: Only 20% of self-service facilities have enough documentation, while 70% of full-service facilities document their experiments sufficiently.
source: Only 20% of self-service facilities have enough documentation, while 70% of full-service facilities document their experiments sufficiently.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages for documentation practices.

claim: About 37% of facilities feel that the communication with their users needs to be improved.
source: About 37% of facilities feel that the communication with their users needs to be improved (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific percentage for this perception.

claim: About half of self-service facilities estimate that their users use provided information only rarely or just sometimes.
source: About half of self-service facilities estimate that their users use this information only rarely or just sometimes (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript states this estimate and references Figure 4B.

claim: Over 70% and 95% of facilities (full-service and self-service respectively) do not have full knowledge of how samples are prepared.
source: Furthermore, issues with communication and trust affect another aspect critical for good quality research – the evaluation of sample quality (also discussed in the sections research quality above). Over 70% and 95% of facilities (full-service and self-service respectively) do not have a full knowledge how samples are prepared (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages for knowledge of sample preparation.

claim: Less than 20% of users of self-service facilities contact the facility (always or often) before publishing their results.
source: Finally, less than 20% of users of self-service facilities contact the facility (always or often) before publishing their results (Figure 4D), whereas as facilities firmly believe that doing this would improve the quality of the published data (Figure 2G).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific percentage for user contact before publication.

claim: The words 'responsible' or 'responsibility' were mentioned 123 times in total in free text responses.
source: The words "responsible" or "responsibility" were mentioned 123 times in total, referring to issues ranging from experimental design to publication.
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific count of keyword mentions.

claim: Core facilities are an effective way of making expensive experimental equipment available to a large number of researchers.
source: Core facilities are an effective way of making expensive experimental equipment available to a large number of researchers, and are thus well placed to contribute to efforts to promote good research practices.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general characterization of core facilities.

claim: Core facilities provide access to state-of-the-art equipment and advanced skills in a cost- and time-effective way.
source: Core facilities have a central position in many areas of research in the life sciences because: (i) they provide access to state-of-the-art equipment and advanced skills in a cost- and time-effective way; (ii) they develop new technologies and transfer their technical and research expertise to the numerous scientists; (iii) they connect institutions and foster collaborations and interdisciplinary research (Meder et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites Meder et al., 2016 for this characterization of core facilities.

claim: Core facilities develop new technologies and transfer their technical and research expertise to numerous scientists.
source: Core facilities have a central position in many areas of research in the life sciences because: (i) they provide access to state-of-the-art equipment and advanced skills in a cost- and time-effective way; (ii) they develop new technologies and transfer their technical and research expertise to the numerous scientists; (iii) they connect institutions and foster collaborations and interdisciplinary research (Meder et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites Meder et al., 2016 for this characterization of core facilities.

claim: Core facilities connect institutions and foster collaborations and interdisciplinary research.
source: Core facilities have a central position in many areas of research in the life sciences because: (i) they provide access to state-of-the-art equipment and advanced skills in a cost- and time-effective way; (ii) they develop new technologies and transfer their technical and research expertise to the numerous scientists; (iii) they connect institutions and foster collaborations and interdisciplinary research (Meder et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites Meder et al., 2016 for this characterization of core facilities.

claim: Core facilities generate a substantial fraction of the scientific data at some institutions.
source: Core facilities also generate a substantial fraction of the scientific data at some institutions, thereby offering protection against bias in the design and analysis of experiments, and supporting transparency, rigor and reproducibility.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a general observation about core facilities.

claim: Concerns about reproducibility in various areas of research have been growing for more than a decade.
source: Concerns about reproducibility in various areas of research have been growing for more than a decade (Eisner, 2018; Ioannidis, 2005; Ioannidis et al., 2014; Prinz et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple sources to support this claim about reproducibility concerns.

claim: Possible causes for a lack of reproducibility include selective reporting, the pressure to publish, and the need for better training in the design and analysis of experiments.
source: Possible causes for a lack of reproducibility include selective reporting, the pressure to publish, and the need for better training in the design and analysis of experiments (Baker, 2016; Smaldino and McElreath, 2016), and the scientific community has developed various guidelines to promote rigorous and transparent research practice (Bespalov et al., 2020; Dirnagl et al., 2018; Freedman et al., 2017; Munafò et al., 2017; Nosek et al., 2015; Wilkinson et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites Baker, 2016 and Smaldino and McElreath, 2016 for causes of irreproducibility.

claim: The scientific community has developed various guidelines to promote rigorous and transparent research practice.
source: Possible causes for a lack of reproducibility include selective reporting, the pressure to publish, and the need for better training in the design and analysis of experiments (Baker, 2016; Smaldino and McElreath, 2016), and the scientific community has developed various guidelines to promote rigorous and transparent research practice (Bespalov et al., 2020; Dirnagl et al., 2018; Freedman et al., 2017; Munafò et al., 2017; Nosek et al., 2015; Wilkinson et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple sources for guidelines promoting rigorous research.

claim: The ABRF surveyed over 200 core facilities to assess how they implemented NIH guidelines on scientific rigor and reproducibility.
source: The Association of Biomolecular Resource Facilities (ABRF) surveyed over 200 core facilities to assess how they implemented guidelines from the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) on scientific rigor and reproducibility and whether these guidelines influenced services and technology development (Knudtson et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites Knudtson et al., 2019 for the ABRF survey.

claim: The main factors and challenges affecting rigor and reproducibility in the ABRF survey were the lack of training, mentorship, expertise, or oversight, poor sample quality, inadequate standardization of protocols or guidelines and data analysis, poor experimental design, and time pressure.
source: The main factors and challenges affecting the rigor and reproducibility were "the lack of training, mentorship, expertise, or oversight", "poor sample quality", "inadequate standardization of protocols or guidelines, and data analysis", "poor experimental design" and "time pressure".
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from the ABRF survey.

claim: In the ABRF survey, the lack of interest from customers and the lack of authority was considered a hindrance to reproducible research.
source: In addition, the lack of interest from customers and the lack of authority was considered a hindrance to reproducible research.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from the ABRF survey.

claim: The most frequent tools used by facilities to improve rigor in the ABRF survey were quality control and standard operation procedures.
source: The most frequent tools used by facilities to improve rigor were quality control and standard operation procedures.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from the ABRF survey.

claim: The survey had a 28% participation rate.
source: We received 276 total forms (28% participation rate), 253 of which were complete.
evidence: The manuscript provides the participation rate calculation.

claim: The sample size of 253 respondents from 1000 core facilities corresponds to a 5.3% margin of error at 95% confidence level.
source: Assuming an equal (1:1) answer distribution (the worst-case scenario), the sample size of 253 respondents from 1000 core facilities (population) corresponds to a 5.3% margin of error at 95% confidence level.
evidence: The manuscript provides the calculated margin of error.

claim: Full-service facilities are those offering an 'all-inclusive service' where facility staff execute the experiment (with or without data analysis).
source: We call full-service facilities those offering an "all-inclusive service", where facility staff execute the experiment (with or without data analysis).
evidence: The manuscript defines full-service facilities.

claim: Self-service facilities provide and maintain an infrastructure where users have access to equipment, training and expert advice.
source: Self-service facilities provide and maintain an infrastructure where users have access to equipment, training and expert advice. (Such facilities were called user laboratories in Meder et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript defines self-service facilities and cites Meder et al., 2016.

claim: At hybrid-service facilities experiments are performed by facility staff and users.
source: At hybrid-service facilities experiments are performed by facility staff and users.
evidence: The manuscript defines hybrid-service facilities.

claim: The majority of facilities that responded offer training and guidance on experimental design, sample preparation, data analysis and help troubleshooting.
source: The majority of facilities that responded offer training and guidance on experimental design, sample preparation, data analysis and help troubleshooting.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes survey findings about services offered.

claim: Core facilities offer support in writing relevant sections of publications.
source: They also offer support in writing relevant sections of publications.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a service offered by facilities.

claim: Full-service facilities tend to train their users less and consider training less important compared to other facility types.
source: On the other hand, the full-service facilities tend to train their users less, they consider training less important and provide primarily theoretical training (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references figures.

claim: Only half of full-service facilities provide guidance on how to analyze raw data because they analyze the data themselves.
source: Only a half of full-service facilities provide guidance how to analyze raw data, because they analyze the data themselves (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references figures.

claim: Training and communicating with users are the most important factors for achieving research quality according to core facilities.
source: As can be seen from the Figure 2A, the most prominent ones are training and communicating with users, followed by having enough qualified staff, as well as up-to-date and well-maintained equipment.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 2A.

claim: Hiring more staff and purchasing/maintaining equipment are the aspects most in need of improvement according to core facilities.
source: From these factors, hiring more staff and purchasing/maintaining equipment are the most in need of improvement.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from the survey.

claim: Management was mentioned at many different levels including facility, projects, samples, data, IT infrastructure, documentation or automation.
source: Management was mentioned at many different levels: facility, projects, samples, data, IT infrastructure, documentation or automation (see the section on management).
evidence: The manuscript describes the different levels at which management was mentioned.

claim: About half of the facilities that responded did not have enough funding and/or enough staff.
source: About half of the facilities that responded did not have enough funding and/or enough staff (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references a figure.

claim: Quality control of data analysis is usually performed by having the data checked by another staff member at the facility.
source: Quality control of data analysis is usually performed by having the data checked by another staff member at the facility. It can also involve discussing the results with the user (or their principal investigator; PI), or using internal standards and quality control samples (data not shown).
evidence: The manuscript describes methods of quality control for data analysis.

claim: Core facilities are often not informed about upcoming publications.
source: However, core facilities are often not even informed about the upcoming publication (see the section on communication below).
evidence: The manuscript states this as a finding from the survey.

claim: A management software is the tool most frequently used by facilities to achieve research quality.
source: A management software is the tool most frequently used by facilities to achieve research quality (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references a figure.

claim: About 35% of facilities are using facility management software (PPMS, iLab, Open IRIS or Agendo).
source: About 35% are using facility management software (PPMS, iLab, Open IRIS or Agendo), 35% are using data management software (LIMS or ELN), and 4% of are using both.
evidence: The manuscript provides percentages for software usage.

claim: About 35% of facilities are using data management software (LIMS or ELN).
source: About 35% are using facility management software (PPMS, iLab, Open IRIS or Agendo), 35% are using data management software (LIMS or ELN), and 4% of are using both.
evidence: The manuscript provides percentages for software usage.

claim: 4% of facilities are using both facility management software and data management software.
source: About 35% are using facility management software (PPMS, iLab, Open IRIS or Agendo), 35% are using data management software (LIMS or ELN), and 4% of are using both.
evidence: The manuscript provides percentages for software usage.

claim: PPMS is the most used management software in self-service facilities.
source: PPMS is the most used management software in self-service facilities, while iLab, open IRIS and Agendo dominate in full-service facilities (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references a figure.

claim: iLab, open IRIS and Agendo dominate in full-service facilities.
source: PPMS is the most used management software in self-service facilities, while iLab, open IRIS and Agendo dominate in full-service facilities (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references a figure.

claim: A quarter of facilities uses software solutions mentioned only once or twice in the survey.
source: Notably, a quarter of facilities uses software solutions mentioned only once or twice in our survey ("other" in Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references a figure.

claim: 50% of full-service facilities believe data management plans would be useful.
source: Another 50% of full-service facilities believe it would be useful, while only 20% of self-service do.
evidence: The manuscript provides percentages for beliefs about data management plans.

claim: Only 20% of self-service facilities believe data management plans would be useful.
source: Another 50% of full-service facilities believe it would be useful, while only 20% of self-service do.
evidence: The manuscript provides percentages for beliefs about data management plans.

claim: About half of respondents had implemented data management measures to ensure that data are complete, attributable, reusable, compatible, searchable and findable.
source: Looking into the different aspects of data management, we saw that about half of respondents had implemented data management measures to ensure that data are complete, attributable, reusable, compatible, searchable and findable (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references a figure.

claim: One half of self-service facilities does not actually know how the experiments are documented.
source: Importantly, one half of self-service facilities does not actually know, how the experiments are documented.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding about documentation knowledge.

claim: Communication between facility staff and users is mostly done through emails and/or in person.
source: Communication between facility staff and users is mostly done through emails and/or in person, facilities say it could be improved by using a communication management software or a chat/discussion platform, and by actively motivating users to cooperate and read the information provided (data not shown).
evidence: The manuscript describes communication methods and improvement suggestions.

claim: Users use the provided information more frequently in hybrid-service and full-service facilities, which is likely due to the need to conform to the facility's specific instructions for sample preparation.
source: Users use the provided information more frequently in hybrid-service and full-service facilities, which is likely due to the need to conform to the facility's specific instructions for sample preparation.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the data based on logical inference.

claim: The survey results show that core facilities are generally invested in implementing best research practices, support transparency, rigor and reproducibility and protect against cognitive bias.
source: Our results show that core facilities are generally invested in implementing best research practices, support transparency, rigor and reproducibility and protect against cognitive bias, which corroborates the ABRF survey's conclusions (Knudtson et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the overall findings and cites the ABRF survey.

claim: The ABRF survey identified the lack of training, mentorship or oversight as the main factors contributing to the lack of compliance with rigorous and reproducible research.
source: The ABRF survey identified the lack of training, mentorship or oversight as the main factors contributing to the lack of compliance with rigorous and reproducible research.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from the ABRF survey.

claim: Respondents to both surveys listed mostly identical tools to improve research quality.
source: In both surveys, respondents listed mostly identical tools to improve research quality.
evidence: The manuscript compares findings between the two surveys.

claim: Poor sample quality and lack of training were the major challenges in the ABRF survey.
source: While funding and lack of staff was most critical for our respondents, it was poor sample quality and lack of training in the ABRF survey (Knudtson et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites the ABRF survey for these challenges.

claim: Insufficient funding can directly or indirectly affect the research quality at multiple levels.
source: It affects not only the ability to purchase and maintain state-of-the-art equipment, but perhaps even more importantly, it can directly or indirectly affect the research quality at multiple levels (Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of how funding affects quality and references Figure 6.

claim: The inability to hire, train and retain enough qualified staff can lead to slow processing of samples, insufficient quality monitoring and poor interaction with users.
source: For example, the inability to hire, train and retain enough qualified staff can lead to slow processing of samples, insufficient quality monitoring and poor interaction with users, which in turn leads to loss of the users' trust and respect.
evidence: The manuscript provides a logical chain of consequences from insufficient staffing.

claim: Insufficient funding can result in an inefficient daily facility management, depriving the staff of time and preventing them from engaging in technology development and publication output.
source: Another consequence of insufficient funding can be an inefficient daily facility management, depriving the staff of the already limited time and thus preventing them to engage in other tasks such as technology development to maintain state-of-the-art techniques and publication output, which ironically can result in funding reduction in the future.
evidence: The manuscript provides a logical chain of consequences from insufficient funding.

claim: Core facilities should provide information and advice on the experimental design and encourage their users to follow good research practices.
source: CFs should provide information and advice on the experimental design and encourage their users to follow good research practices. They should check the experimental design and reject any ill-designed project.
evidence: The manuscript provides recommendations based on survey findings.

claim: Core facilities should control sample quality before starting the experiment and reject samples of poor quality.
source: CFs should control sample quality before starting the experiment and reject samples of poor quality. In case of limiting or rare samples, CFs should discuss with their users what consequences the sample quality will have on data interpretation and if the experiment should continue.
evidence: The manuscript provides recommendations based on survey findings.

claim: Core facilities and PIs should decide who will be responsible for checking data analysis.
source: CFs and PIs should decide who will be responsible for checking data analysis.
evidence: The manuscript provides recommendations based on survey findings.

claim: Core facilities should be informed before the data produced at the facility are submitted for publication to have the possibility to check them if they wish to.
source: CFs should be informed before the data produced at the CF are submitted for publication to have the possibility to check them if they wish to.
evidence: The manuscript provides recommendations based on survey findings.

claim: The proposed checkpoints need to be adjusted to the needs of each facility.
source: The proposed check points need to be adjusted to the needs of each facility.
evidence: The manuscript provides guidance on implementing recommendations.

claim: Blinding and randomization are very important aspects of experimental design in animal core facilities.
source: For example, blinding and randomization are very important aspects of experimental design in animal core facilities.
evidence: The manuscript provides an example of facility-specific considerations.

claim: Core facilities with a large number of users might not have the capacity to perform the data analysis and publication checkpoints.
source: The core facilities with a large number of users might not have the capacity to perform the data analysis and publication checkpoints.
evidence: The manuscript provides a consideration for implementing recommendations.

claim: The data analysis checkpoint can be assigned to experienced PIs or other qualified scientists outside of the facility.
source: In this case, the data analysis checkpoint can be assigned to experienced PIs or other qualified scientists outside of the facility (e.g. statistician, bioinformatician).
evidence: The manuscript provides an alternative approach for implementing recommendations.

claim: The publication checkpoint is the least important, as editors and reviewers will also be involved.
source: The publication checkpoint is the least important, as editors and reviewers will also be involved.
evidence: The manuscript provides a judgment about the relative importance of checkpoints.

claim: The facility should always be informed about the publications, as these are often required to secure further funding.
source: However, the facility should always be informed about the publications, as these are often required to secure further funding.
evidence: The manuscript provides a practical reason for informing facilities about publications.

claim: Only a precise and relevant documentation can guarantee data traceability.
source: In addition to the above listed checkpoints, only a precise and relevant documentation can guarantee data traceability.
evidence: The manuscript makes a statement about the necessity of documentation for traceability.

claim: Users of self-service facilities would particularly benefit from the expertise of facility staff.
source: Users of self-service facilities would particularly benefit from the expertise of facility staff as most core facilities offer information to users on all stages of the research process (from experimental design to publication).
evidence: The manuscript provides an inference based on survey findings.

claim: Management software was rated as one of the best tools to improve research quality.
source: Management software was rated as one of the best tools to improve research quality (which includes ensuring the traceability of the data collected).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes survey findings about tools for quality improvement.

claim: The implementation and cost of management software are the biggest obstacles preventing wider usage.
source: The software solutions used by core facilities are very heterogeneous with the implementation and cost being the biggest obstacles preventing wider usage.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes survey findings about barriers to software adoption.

claim: There is currently no management software allowing the full management of the facility from booking scheduling to billing.
source: Importantly, some respondents noted that there is currently no management software allowing the full management of the facility, from booking scheduling, experimental design, data acquisition and analysis to billing.
evidence: The manuscript reports feedback from survey respondents.

claim: Development of comprehensive management software would likely reduce the time facilities lose by switching between incompatible software packages and increase the traceability of the data.
source: Development of such software would likely reduce the time facilities lose by switching between two or more incompatible software packages and increase the traceability of the data.
evidence: The manuscript provides a prediction about the benefits of comprehensive software.

claim: An ideal management software must be user-friendly, simple and fast.
source: Critically, an ideal management software must be user-friendly, simple and fast, as users are not willing to use an overly complicated and time demanding software and might refuse to cooperate.
evidence: The manuscript provides requirements for effective management software based on user behavior.

claim: Many core facilities require specific solutions capable of handling the particular type and amount of data they produce.
source: Apart from the general data management described above, many core facilities require specific solutions capable of handling the particular type and amount of data they produce.
evidence: The manuscript describes the need for specialized data management solutions.

claim: Efficiently storing and querying large amounts of data from sequencing, microscopy or mass spectroscopy experiments each require tailored software solutions.
source: For example, efficiently storing and querying large amounts of data from sequencing, microscopy or mass spectroscopy experiments each require tailored software solutions.
evidence: The manuscript provides examples of data types requiring specialized solutions.

claim: The general and specialized data management systems should be interconnected and allow the attribution of the appropriate data set to each experiment or user.
source: However, the general and specialized data management systems should be interconnected and allow the attribution of the appropriate data set to each experiment or user.

source: Deficient communication between facility staff and their users can directly affect science quality.

source: One third of core facilities are not satisfied with the current situation and wishes to improve the communication with their users.

source: First, handling questions or requests from many users on an individual basis can easily overload a facility if it is understaffed.

source: In this regard, a tailored management software can lighten the load on the facility staff.

source: First, relevant quality checkpoints should be introduced at sample submission, after data analysis and also just before publication.

source: Second, data management should be further improved in most core facilities, and the use of management software would be beneficial.

source: Second, data management should be further improved in most core facilities, and the use of management software would be beneficial.
